problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand per store and product for 400 stores and 30,000 products. Monday forecasts for the next eight weeks feed replenishment. Nightly till sales arrive in a warehouse managed by central IT, which the three-person data-science team cannot change.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

points.description: The system ingests row-level features through batch ETL and runs preparation, extraction, parallel candidate training, evaluation, and deployment as an orchestrated pipeline on managed infrastructure. Commit-triggered releases build and test artifacts across stages, while comprehensive traceability governs datasets, runs, experiments, pipeline designs, deployment health, and scheduled batch predictions, with production logging and security observability. Trade-off: It gains repeatability, scalable candidate comparison, governed releases, and operational visibility, but gives up low-latency predictions and may increase batch-processing delay and managed-platform dependence. Batch-oriented execution also limits responsiveness to rapidly changing data.

Batch ETL supplies row-level features to a standalone managed cloud ML service. A composable, DataOps-centered toolchain and manually run scripts cover preparation, training, validation, and deployment; versioned pipelines and experiments support gated promotion, vertically scaled training, scheduled batch scoring, and periodic health checks. Trade-off: It favors simplicity, reproducibility, controlled releases, and adequate scaling for infrequently changing batch models, but sacrifices real-time predictions, distributed training, continuous monitoring, rapid adaptation, and end-to-end automation.

An orchestrated ML pipeline ingests batch row-level features, runs across managed and pluggable engines, and automates preparation through deployment. It uses checkpointed partitioned training, end-to-end versioning, progressive releases with rollback, precomputes predictions for serving, and automatically recovers operational failures. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, portability, recoverability, governed reproducibility, and safer releases. It gives up real-time prediction freshness and incurs complexity from multi-engine coordination, extensive lifecycle governance, and checkpoint/recovery machinery.

Source systems are batch-extracted, transformed, and loaded as row-level features into an orchestrated, managed ML pipeline. The pipeline concurrently trains candidate models, governs versioned data, artifacts, experiments, and metadata, promotes releases through progressively stronger environment gates, schedules batch scoring to storage or analytics systems, and provides production logging, security, monitoring, and observability. Trade-off: This favors reproducibility, controlled promotion, candidate comparison, and operational governance, but gives up real-time prediction freshness and incurs batch-processing, orchestration, and concurrent-training compute costs.

Source records are batch-extracted, transformed into row-level features, and fed through an orchestrated, managed pipeline for preparation, parallel candidate training, evaluation, and deployment. Commit-triggered release automation promotes tested artifacts through stages, while end-to-end versioning governs datasets, experiments, dependencies, and model health; scheduled batch scoring writes predictions to storage and automated recovery handles failures. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, governance, candidate comparison, and reduced operational intervention. It gives up low-latency or continuously fresh predictions and may incur greater compute and infrastructure cost from parallel training and managed services.

Batch ETL feeds a managed, orchestrated ML pipeline that automates preparation, parallel candidate training, evaluation, deployment, and lifecycle traceability. It produces periodically refreshed offline predictions, while progressive releases support rollback and automated recovery handles production failures. Trade-off: This gains repeatability, comparison of candidates, operational resilience, and governed traceability, but offline serving sacrifices prediction freshness and immediate responsiveness. Parallel training and comprehensive automation can increase compute and operational complexity, while managed infrastructure may constrain execution choices.

ETL batch-loads row-level features into a standalone managed cloud ML platform, where manually coordinated workflows train multiple candidates in parallel and move through validation and deployment. Versioned pipelines, artifacts, and experiments support comparison and reproducibility; gated releases deploy scheduled batch scoring, store results for analytics, and trigger periodic health checks. Trade-off: This favors simplicity, controlled promotion, reproducibility, and efficient offline comparison, but sacrifices freshness, continuous orchestration, real-time predictions, and continuous adaptation. Manual coordination increases execution and coordination effort.

An ETL layer supplies row-level features to an orchestrated, repeatable ML pipeline running across managed services and selectable execution engines. Automated lifecycle and progressive-release controls govern versioned experiments, artifacts, datasets, and deployments; fault-tolerant partitioned training produces models that are scheduled for batch scoring and monitored with automated recovery. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, resilient training, controlled rollback, and automation across heterogeneous infrastructure. It gives up immediate prediction freshness and adds coordination complexity across multiple engines and recovery paths.

A managed, orchestrated pipeline automates preparation through deployment, trains candidate models in parallel, governs artifacts and metadata end to end, and progressively releases selected versions with rollback. Scheduled batch scoring writes predictions to downstream storage or analytics systems, while production logging, security controls, monitoring, and observability support operations and adaptation. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, safer releases, systematic model comparison, and operational visibility, but gives up real-time prediction freshness and incurs greater compute, orchestration, and governance overhead.

Source records are batch-extracted into features, then processed by a managed, orchestrated pipeline that prepares data, trains parallel candidates, evaluates them, and governs artifacts and metadata end to end. The selected model is released progressively with rollback support, serves predictions on a schedule to storage or analytics systems, and has feature and input drift monitored in production. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, automated lifecycle control, comparative training, and safer releases, but batch ingestion and scheduled serving reduce prediction freshness and responsiveness. Parallel training and comprehensive governance also increase compute and operational overhead.

approaches.idea: What if a managed, orchestrated pipeline and lifecycle traceability carry the recurring weekly workload and model comparison?
What if a small team keeps the workflow mostly script-driven and uses a lightweight managed service with periodic review?
approaches.dropped_because: Manual transitions and periodic review cannot support the one-week, approval-only production path and rapid failure visibility without replacing the approach's defining manual coordination.

approaches.idea: What if hybrid engines, partitioned recovery, and progressive rollback prioritize resilience and portability?
What if the system emphasizes reproducible candidate experiments and offline forecasts, then uses recovery and rollback for operations?

trajectory.hypothesis: A managed, orchestrated pipeline with candidate parallelism and end-to-end traceability should support R1–R3, Q1, and Q2; batch scoring and observability may help Q3, though six-hour runtime and atomic delivery remain unverified.

tradeoffs.note: Managed lifecycle automation reduces recurring manual operations but adds platform concepts for a small team to learn and operate.

trajectory.observation: The checked point had no required-dimension warnings but no source attested the complete combination. Its component values support automation and traceability; neither six-hour capacity nor all-machine onboarding is demonstrated.

trajectory.hypothesis: A simpler managed service and manual workflow should reduce setup burden for C1 and Q4, but may struggle with R3, Q2, and fast failure response.

tradeoffs.note: Manual transitions and periodic checks limit setup and operational tooling but cannot provide the requested approval-only release path or rapid failure notification.

trajectory.observation: The low-complexity seed misses stressed qualities due to manual execution and periodic review, but parallel comparisons could improve R3 without changing the workflow's basic shape. Its vertically scaled training has no measured six-hour result.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid infrastructure, end-to-end versioning, checkpointed training, rollback, and recovery should strengthen R2, Q1, and Q3 while retaining R3; operational complexity may challenge C1 and Q4.

tradeoffs.note: Selectable engines, fault-tolerant partitioning, and offline scoring offer execution and recovery options but add systems and recovery concepts for a small team.

trajectory.observation: This point preserves a full experiment and reproduction path and adds recovery mechanisms. The workspace does not establish a 15-minute alert or atomic handoff, and hybrid operations could burden the team.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing commit-triggered staged releases with environment-gated deployment should retain automation while making explicit approval compatible with Q2 and safer promotion.

tradeoffs.note: Environment gates preserve validation and approval while the managed release platform adds concepts for an incoming teammate to learn.

trajectory.observation: End-to-end governance improves the fit for historical reproduction. The described gates do not guarantee a one-week delivery interval or quantify run capacity.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping managed infrastructure while adopting commit-triggered release automation and parallel candidate training may reduce C1 and Q4 burdens while preserving recovery and evaluation.

tradeoffs.note: Managed pipeline infrastructure avoids operating a multi-engine substrate but adds a platform for an incoming teammate to learn.

trajectory.observation: The point retains the strong reproduction and comparison story while lowering the hybrid infrastructure burden. Recovery and logging still do not prove partial-output prevention or a 15-minute alert.

trajectory.hypothesis: A candidate-experiment-centered point with offline forecasts, rollback, and recovery may retain reproducibility and comparison while prioritizing operational resilience.

tradeoffs.note: Precomputed offline results match periodic replenishment delivery, while operating a managed platform adds onboarding concepts for the team.

trajectory.observation: The combination remains unattested, but its elements cover offline prediction, versioned experiments, and automated recovery. Exact deadline and reliability targets still need verification.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding parallel candidate training should improve R3 while retaining the lean, manually coordinated shape.

tradeoffs.note: Concurrent candidate training supports comparisons but consumes additional compute, with no capacity measurement against the six-hour window.

trajectory.observation: Parallelizing experiments improves comparison but does not remove manual handoffs, so the approach still misses Q2 and Q3. B is dropped before the final round because fixing its missed automation and notification needs would replace its defining manual coordination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Retaining hybrid engines, checkpointed partitioning, and rollback while switching to scheduled batch predictions should better match the weekly delivery contract.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid execution and partition recovery add resilience options but increase operational complexity for the three-person team.

trajectory.observation: Scheduled scoring aligns with weekly replenishment and retains reproduction and model comparison. No evidence specifies whole-file publication semantics, alert latency, or a six-hour runtime.

trajectory.hypothesis: Moving D from offline predictions to scheduled batch deployment and broader operational observability should fit the weekly handoff and strengthen failure awareness.

tradeoffs.note: Scheduled batch delivery matches the weekly cadence, while managed platform operations add learning and maintenance work for the team.

trajectory.observation: The managed point preserves experiment governance and rollback while specifying scheduled output and observability. The logging value does not state a 15-minute notification threshold.

trajectory.hypothesis: Switching A's monitoring choice to input and feature drift monitoring should improve detection of upstream or feature changes while retaining staged weekly output, comparisons, and reproducibility.

tradeoffs.note: Input and feature-drift monitoring improves change visibility but adds an operational view and associated concepts for a new teammate.

trajectory.observation: The final refinement adds explicit input and feature-drift coverage. Runtime capacity, individual-machine onboarding, alert timing, and atomic output remain unproven by the checked point.

alternatives.name: Governed managed weekly pipeline
alternatives.summary: Use a managed, orchestrated pipeline with end-to-end lifecycle governance, parallel candidate comparisons, scheduled delivery, progressive rollback, and input-drift monitoring.

choices.reason: Batch ETL uses the nightly warehouse data path without requiring a change to the warehouse. Evidence is reported in Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline: How to build scalable Machine Learning systems - Part 2/2.
Repeatable stages automate the recurring run and evaluation workflow. Evidence is reported in MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning.
Managed pipeline-centered infrastructure limits the need for a separate platform operations team. Evidence is reported in Architecting a Machine Learning System for Risk.
Automating recurring lifecycle work reduces manual transitions. Evidence is reported in MLOps Principles.
Progressive releases with rollback support controlled promotion after approval. Evidence is reported in Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture.

End-to-end versioning ties datasets, experiments, artifacts, and runs together for reproduction and comparison. Evidence is reported in MLOps: What It Is, Why it Matters, and How To Implement It (from a Data Scientist Perspective).

Scheduled batch prediction matches the weekly replenishment delivery pattern. Evidence is reported in Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline: How to build scalable Machine Learning systems - Part 2/2.

Parallel candidate training supports comparison within the overnight window, though actual duration needs measurement. Evidence is reported in Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline: How to build scalable Machine Learning systems - Part 2/2.
Feature and input drift monitoring can surface data changes that threaten a run. Evidence is reported in Machine Learning Monitoring: What It Is, and What We Are Missing.
choices.fit_note: The value covers input and feature drift; it does not specify a 15-minute notification or prevent partial forecasts from being published.

considered.reason: Environment-gated automation makes approval explicit, but the final design favors rollback during progressive rollout.
Comprehensive traceability was an earlier choice; end-to-end reproducible governance covers a wider set of reproducibility concerns.

relations.note: The point selects an ingestion mechanism as required before deciding workflow coordination.

alternatives.summary: Use a repeatable pipeline across managed and specialized engines, with partitioned recovery, end-to-end governance, rollback, and scheduled batch scoring.

Orchestration provides repeatable preparation, training, and evaluation stages. Evidence is reported in Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture.
Selectable engines offer runtime flexibility for specialized or resilient execution. Evidence is reported in Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture.
Automated lifecycle workflows reduce repeated manual operations. Evidence is reported in Architecting a Machine Learning System for Risk.

adrs.title: Coordinate and host the forecasting workflow
adrs.context: The pipeline must run weekly and compare model candidates while a three-person team works with an unchanged warehouse. A managed workflow can reduce platform operations, while manual scripts are easy to start but leave recurring transitions and releases to the team.

options.name: Managed orchestrated lifecycle
pros: Repeatable preparation, training, evaluation, and deployment stages
Less self-operated infrastructure and recurring manual work
cons: Managed platform and governance still require learning and upkeep
options.reason: This is the best fit for a small team that needs recurring runs and rapid candidate promotion.

options.name: Hybrid multi-engine automation
pros: Execution can use specialized or selectable runtimes
Keeps an automated workflow
cons: Adds engine integration and operations burden
options.reason: Choose this when flexibility and recovery options outweigh the added platform complexity.

options.name: Manual scripts with composable tooling
pros: Simple entry point for a small team
Can use a standalone managed service
cons: Manual transitions undermine approval-only promotion and rapid operational response
options.reason: The manual coordination premise misses Q2 and Q3.

options.name: Batch ETL from the existing warehouse
pros: Uses batch row-level features from external data sources
Fits the existing nightly data arrival pattern
cons: The runtime and data volume still need validation
options.reason: All alternatives rely on the nightly batch data path without changing the warehouse.

adrs.title: Reproduce runs and govern model releases
adrs.context: The team must replay historical forecasts and test candidate models before promotion. Versioning only experiments is lighter, while lifecycle-wide governance provides more complete linkage among data, artifacts, and runs. Release controls need to automate promotion while retaining approval and recovery paths.

options.name: End-to-end versioning with progressive rollback
pros: Links data, artifacts, runs, and experiments for reproduction
Supports progressive production release and rollback
cons: Lifecycle metadata and governance add maintenance overhead
options.reason: It best supports historical replay, candidate comparison, and safe promotion across the live alternatives.

options.name: Pipeline and experiment version control with gated promotion
pros: Versions alternatives and training results
Makes environment approval gates explicit
cons: Covers fewer lifecycle links than end-to-end governance
options.reason: This was the leaner seed, but it does not make the rest of the manual workflow suitable for the required release pace.

options.name: Comprehensive traceability with commit-triggered release
pros: Tracks runs, datasets, metadata, and deployment health
Automates staged build and promotion
cons: The final live points prefer rollback-oriented progressive release and broader end-to-end reproducibility
options.reason: Useful first point, refined to stronger lifecycle governance and recovery-oriented release behavior.

adrs.title: Produce and compare scheduled forecasts
adrs.context: Replenishment consumes a weekly eight-week forecast, and candidate ideas need historical comparison. Scheduled batch scoring matches the cadence, but the space contains no measured workload capacity for the six-hour window.

options.name: Scheduled batch scoring with parallel candidates
pros: Matches the weekly delivery pattern
Supports concurrent candidate comparison
cons: Concurrent training can consume more compute; exact runtime is unknown
options.reason: This combines the production cadence and offline model comparison, subject to a workload benchmark for C2.

options.name: Offline precomputation with fault-tolerant partitioning
pros: Precomputes predictions for periodic use
Checkpointing supports recovery of partitioned training
cons: Does not describe the downstream scheduled publication as directly
options.reason: The hybrid seed offered resilience, but scheduled batch deployment maps more closely to the weekly handoff.

options.name: Scheduled batch scoring with vertical scaling
pros: Simple batch deployment and larger-machine scaling
cons: Candidate comparison is less parallel and capacity remains unmeasured
options.reason: This option gives less support to rapid comparison of model ideas.

options.name: Offline precomputation with parallel candidates
pros: Precomputes predictions for periodic use
Supports concurrent candidate comparison
cons: Offline result generation still needs a scheduled publication step
options.reason: Explored as a candidate-centered approach, then refined to explicit scheduled batch deployment.

adrs.title: Observe and recover production runs
adrs.context: Failures must become visible quickly, and incomplete results must never reach replenishment. The space has monitoring and recovery alternatives, but no value specifies a notification service with a 15-minute bound or transactional publication of a complete forecast.

options.name: Input drift monitoring and operations logging
pros: Can identify changing or anomalous inputs
cons: Does not guarantee an alert threshold or atomic publication
options.reason: Adds input-change coverage to a point with automated workflow and release controls.

options.name: Production logging and security observability
pros: Provides production logging and operational observability
cons: No specified alert timing or output completeness guarantee
options.reason: A broad operational visibility choice suits the experiment-led batch alternative.

options.name: Automated failure recovery with hybrid execution
pros: Supports recovery from operational failures
cons: Recovery does not ensure a human is notified within 15 minutes

options.name: Periodic health checks
pros: Offers a light recurring review process
cons: Periodic review cannot ensure rapid failure notification
options.reason: The seed point misses the reliability target because its checks are not continuous.
